subtitle: How Warangal Turned Steel and Scripture into Song

panels.shot: epic split-frame wide, half battlefield, half temple dance hall
panels.action: Jayapa Senani stands armored with a palm-leaf manuscript in hand, while Tikkana, robed and composed, faces him with a Mahabharata scroll; behind them rise Warangal’s fort walls and temple pillars crowded with dancing stone figures.

dialogue.text: In Kakatiya Warangal, a general wrote the laws of dance, a poet bent the Mahabharata into Telugu, and between sword and scripture a new memory of the south was born.

i18n.hi: काकतीय वारंगल में एक सेनापति ने नृत्य के नियम लिखे, एक कवि ने महाभारत को तेलुगु में मोड़ा, और तलवार व ग्रंथ के बीच दक्षिण की नई याद जन्मी।

panels.shot: slow push-in on Jayapa in armor watching temple dancers near the Ramappa-style lake
panels.action: Jayapa Senani, in chain-mail and helmet, stands at the edge of a lakeside temple courtyard, watching male and female dancers mid-spin as drummers beat out complex rhythms under carved mandapa pillars.

dialogue.text: Around 1231, as Kakatiya banners snapped over Warangal, their general Jayapa watched dancers move like soldiers, and wondered: could the fury of war itself be written as a dance?

i18n.hi: लगभग 1231 में, जब काकतीय ध्वज वारंगल पर लहरा रहे थे, सेनापति जयपा ने नर्तकों को सैनिकों-सा चलते देखा और सोचा: क्या खुद युद्ध का उफान नृत्य में लिखा जा सकता है?

panels.shot: intimate interior wide of Jayapa seated at a low desk with palm-leaf manuscripts
panels.action: In a lamplit chamber, Jayapa Senani sits cross-legged before a stack of palm leaves, stylus poised, looking from a bronze Nataraja to the quiet courtyard beyond, where silhouettes of warriors drill.

dialogue.text: He was no wandering aesthete, but a senani, a commander. Yet his Nrtta Ratnavali set out to catalogue marga and desi dance, courtly grace and martial Perini, with the care of a strategist mapping terrain.

i18n.hi: वो कोई घूमता कलाकार नहीं, सेनानी था। फिर भी उसकी ‘नृत्यरत्नावली’ ने मार्ग और देशी नृत्य, दरबारी लावण्य और युद्धी परिनी को रणभूमि की नक्शेबाज़ी जैसी सूक्ष्मता से दर्ज किया।

panels.shot: diagrammatic overhead wide of dancers and fighters mirroring stances
panels.action: In an open yard, temple dancers leap and stamp in a Perini sequence while nearby Kakatiya soldiers practice lunges and spins; Jayapa stands between them, one hand lifted as if aligning their movements.

dialogue.text: Perini, the desi dance of warriors, stamped tempo into muscle and breath. Jayapa watched bodies remember patterns of attack and retreat, and saw knowledge living not in ink, but in sinew.

i18n.hi: परिनी, योद्धाओं का देशी नृत्य, लय को माँस-पेशियों और साँस में ठोंकता था। जयपा ने देखा कि देह हमले और वापसी की चालें याद रखती है, मानो ज्ञान स्याही नहीं, स्नायु में रहता हो।

panels.shot: close-up on palm-leaf where terms marga and desi are being inscribed
panels.action: A close view of Jayapa’s hand pressing stylus into palm leaf, etching neat Telugu-Kannada script lines beside small drawn stick-figures that show positions of arms and legs.

dialogue.text: So he wrote. Marga, the pan-Indian classical path; desi, the local pulse of the Deccan. He made space for both, a manual where the great treatises met the fierce rhythms of Warangal.

i18n.hi: सो उसने लिखा: मार्ग, अखिल भारतीय शास्त्रीय पथ; देशी, दक्खिन की स्थानीय धड़कन। दोनों के लिए जगह बना दी—ऐसा ग्रंथ जहाँ बड़े शास्त्र वारंगल की तेज़ लयों से मिलते हैं।

panels.shot: formal court wide in Chebrolu, with Ganapati Deva on throne and Jayapa bowing
panels.action: Inside a richly carved hall evoking Chebrolu, Ganapati Deva sits on a high throne flanked by ministers while Jayapa, armored but unhelmeted, offers a bundle of palm leaves in a respectful bow.

dialogue.text: A Chebrolu inscription of 21 April 1235 speaks Jayapa’s name in stone, tying him to royal patronage. In such courts, generals did more than fight; they curated the very arts that honored kings.

i18n.hi: 21 अप्रैल 1235 की चेब्रोलु शिलालेख में जयपा का नाम पत्थर पर उभरता है, जो उसे राजाश्रय से जोड़ता है। ऐसी सभाओं में सेनापति सिर्फ लड़ते नहीं थे, वे राजाओं की महिमा गाने वाली कलाओं के संरक्षक भी थे।

panels.shot: medium shot of temple sculptors studying dancers as Jayapa observes quietly
panels.action: Under a half-finished temple tower, sculptors watch live dancers perform a Perini sequence, then chisel dynamic stone figures into a pillar, while Jayapa stands aside, arms folded, expression intent.

dialogue.text: In the Kakatiya age, palm leaves spoke to stone. The movements Jayapa named were frozen in Ramappa’s pillars, bodies twisted mid-step, so that future eyes could read a dance from silent rock.

i18n.hi: काकतीय युग में ताड़पत्र पत्थर से बोलते थे। जयपा ने जिन भंगिमाओं के नाम दिए, वे रामप्पा के स्तंभों में जड़ हो गईं—देहें आधे कदम पर मुड़ी हुईं, ताकि आने वाली आँखें मौन शिला से नृत्य पढ़ सकें।

panels.shot: time-lapse style composite showing centuries passing from Jayapa’s era to a modern guru
panels.action: A layered image: Jayapa’s manuscript lies beside weathered Ramappa pillars; in the foreground, a 20th-century guru resembling Nataraja Ramakrishna studies the sculpture, manuscript open, students poised to learn.

dialogue.text: Centuries later, Nataraja Ramakrishna would join Jayapa’s text to Ramappa’s sculpture to revive Perini. The general’s manual, once courtly theory, became a map back to a forgotten fire in the body.

i18n.hi: सदियों बाद नटराज रामकृष्ण ने जयपा के ग्रंथ को रामप्पा की मूर्तियों से जोड़कर परिनी को फिर जगा दिया। सेनापति का दरबारी शास्त्र देह की भूली आग तक लौटने का नक्शा बन गया।

panels.shot: transition wide from Warangal to the coastal plains around Nellore
panels.action: The scene shifts from Warangal’s dry fort ramparts to lush coastal fields near Nellore, with a river curving past a modest fort and temple towers rising beyond.

dialogue.text: While Warangal wrote movement into stone, to the east, in Nellore, another Kakatiya-linked world labored over words. There, Tikkana opened the Mahabharata to Telugu-speaking hearts.

i18n.hi: जब वारंगल ने हरकत को पत्थर में लिखा, तब पूर्व में नेल्लूर में एक और काकतीय-बंधी दुनिया शब्दों पर जुटी थी। वहाँ तिक्कन ने महाभारत को तेलुगु दिलों के लिए खोला।

panels.shot: interior scholar’s chamber with Tikkana writing by lamplight
panels.action: In a quiet room lined with palm-leaf bundles, Tikkana sits bareheaded in a simple scholar’s robe, bending over a leaf as an oil lamp flickers and a Sanskrit manuscript lies open beside his Telugu draft.

dialogue.text: Serving the Nellore Chodas, not as a Kakatiya court poet but as their man, Tikkana translated most of the Mahabharata into Telugu. He called his work Andhra Mahabharatam, claiming space for a southern voice.

i18n.hi: नेल्लूर चोडों की सेवा करते हुए—काकतीय दरबार कवि नहीं, उनका अपना आदमी बनकर—तिक्कन ने ज्यादातर महाभारत को तेलुगु में उतारा। उसने इसे ‘आंध्र महाभारतम’ कहा, दक्षिण की आवाज़ के लिए जगह माँगी।

panels.shot: close-up on Tikkana’s thoughtful face as he glances between Sanskrit and Telugu leaves
panels.action: Tikkana’s face is shown in close-up, brows furrowed yet calm, as his eyes move from a neat Sanskrit shloka to his own flowing Telugu lines on another leaf.

dialogue.text: He did not merely swap words from Sanskrit to Telugu. He chose idioms of field and fort, wove local textures into epic scenes, making warriors, queens and sages speak in a tongue of daily life.

i18n.hi: वो सिर्फ संस्कृत शब्दों को तेलुगु में नहीं पलटता। खेत और किले की बोलियाँ चुनता, स्थानीय रंगों से महाकाव्य दृश्य बुनता, ताकि योद्धा, रानी और ऋषि रोज़मर्रा की ज़बान में बोल सकें।

panels.shot: formal audience scene with Tikkana before Ganapati Deva’s court as an envoy
panels.action: Inside a Kakatiya-style durbar, Ganapati Deva sits on his throne while Tikkana, scroll in hand, stands formally as an envoy, a few Nellore retainers behind him, presenting himself with measured dignity.

dialogue.speaker: jayapa_senani_and_tikkana
dialogue.text: I come from Nellore’s Chodas, bearing words – and a tongue that now holds the Mahabharata.

i18n.hi: मैं नेल्लूर के चोडों से आया हूँ, शब्द लेकर – और ऐसी ज़बान जो अब महाभारत को थामे हुए है।

panels.shot: wide shot of mixed audience listening to a recitation of Andhra Mahabharatam
panels.action: In a large hall, villagers, minor nobles and warriors sit in rows as a reciter chants from Tikkana’s Telugu Mahabharata; listeners lean forward, some silently mouthing familiar phrases.

dialogue.text: As his Andhra Mahabharatam spread, epics once bound to Sanskrit halls now echoed in village courtyards. In the Deccan, language itself began to mark belonging, a shared memory of heroes and wars.

i18n.hi: जैसे-जैसे उसकी ‘आंध्र महाभारतम’ फैली, पहले संस्कृत सभाओं तक बाँधीं कथाएँ गाँव के आँगनों में गूँजने लगीं। दक्खिन में भाषा खुद अपनापन बन गई, वीरों और युद्धों की साझा स्मृति।

panels.shot: court interior at Warangal with Prataparudra and Vidyanatha reciting
panels.action: Later Kakatiya ruler Prataparudra sits attentive in a Warangal court as Vidyanatha, a sophisticated Sanskrit poet, recites verses, hand raised in elegant gesture; scribes and scholars line the walls.

dialogue.text: By around 1320, Vidyanatha’s Prataparudriyam praised Prataparudra in polished Sanskrit. It showed a court where high Sanskrit poetics still held prestige, even as Telugu storytelling grew strong outside.

i18n.hi: लगभग 1320 में विद्यनाथ की ‘प्रतापरुद्रियम’ ने प्रतापरुद्र की परिष्कृत संस्कृत में स्तुति की। इससे एक ऐसा दरबार दिखा जहाँ उच्च संस्कृत काव्य-रूचि अभी भी शान थी, जबकि बाहर तेलुगु कथा-धारा मज़बूत हो रही थी।

panels.shot: documentary-style split-screen of scholars debating Telugu identity with backdrop maps
panels.action: Modern scholars stand in a seminar room with maps of the Deccan and projected manuscript images, gesturing as they discuss; the ghost-like overlay of Jayapa, Tikkana, and Vidyanatha appears above.

dialogue.text: Recent historians like Velcheru Narayana Rao, Shulman and Eaton read these texts as clues: Kakatiya times were not just about forts, but about a slow weaving of Telugu literary identity around them.

i18n.hi: नए इतिहासकार जैसे वेल्चेरु नारायणराव, शुल्मन और ईटन इन ग्रंथों को सूत्र मानते हैं: काकतीय समय सिर्फ किलों का नहीं था, बल्कि उन्हीं के इर्द-गिर्द धीमे-धीमे बुनी जा रही तेलुगु साहित्यिक पहचान का भी था।

panels.shot: poetic wide shot of a dancer, a storyteller, and a temple together at dusk
panels.action: At dusk, a Perini dancer stamps in a courtyard, a storyteller recites a Telugu Mahabharata episode to onlookers, and a temple looms behind them, its carved dancers glowing in the fading light.

dialogue.text: Jayapa’s Nrtta Ratnavali met Ramappa’s stone; Tikkana’s Andhra Mahabharatam met village ears; Vidyanatha’s Sanskrit met royal pride. Together, they turned Warangal’s power into layered memory.

i18n.hi: जयपा की ‘नृत्यरत्नावली’ रामप्पा के पत्थर से मिली; तिक्कन की ‘आंध्र महाभारतम’ गाँव के कानों से; विद्यनाथ की संस्कृत राजाभिमान से। साथ मिलकर उन्होंने वारंगल की ताकत को परतदार याद में बदल दिया।

panels.shot: final contemplative low-angle on Jayapa and Tikkana statues facing different directions
panels.action: Two imagined statues stand back-to-back on a plinth: Jayapa, in armor, hands resting on a manuscript; Tikkana, in scholar’s robe, scroll clasped; beyond them stretch a battlefield plain and a river of villages.

dialogue.text: Their lesson endures: a people’s learning does not live in books alone, but also in bodies, songs and tales, and when power falls, these living arts carry its memory forward in their own tongues and steps.

i18n.hi: उनका संदेश आज भी है: किसी जाति की सीख सिर्फ किताबों में नहीं, देह, गीत और कथाओं में भी रहती है, और जब सत्ता गिरती है, तो यही जीवित कलाएँ अपनी ज़बान और चाल में उसकी स्मृति आगे ले जाती हैं।

title_i18n.en: Jayapa Writes the Dance of War

subtitle_i18n.en: How Warangal Turned Steel and Scripture into Song
